did_you_know.text: The chapter presents Gog as the leader of the land of Magog and as the “chief prince of Meshech and Tubal.” Ezekiel is commanded to prophesy against him—that is, to announce in advance his fate and the coming campaign.
The LORD is described as putting “hooks into Gog’s jaws” and leading him into battle with his army. This is an image of control and guidance toward a predetermined destination.
Gog’s army is joined by Persia, Cush, and Put, described as nations equipped with shields and helmets. This emphasizes that the force is a broad coalition, not a single army.
The allies also include Gomer, Beth-togarmah, and many peoples from the far north. The list of nations emphasizes the size and reach of Gog’s camp.

The invasion takes place in the latter days against a land gathered from many peoples after devastation and wars. Its inhabitants are described as people who have returned to the land and are living securely.
Gog plans to attack a land of “unwalled villages”—settlements without walls, gates, or bars. He sees this security situation as an opportunity to take plunder.

Sheba, Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish are not described as fighting against Gog. Instead, they ask whether he has come to seize plunder and carry off spoil. Their response highlights the invasion’s economic motive.

The LORD brings Gog against the land of Israel so that the nations will know him when he reveals his holiness before their eyes through these events. According to the chapter, the campaign also serves to reveal the LORD’s power and holiness.
Gog’s arrival causes a great earthquake in the land of Israel. The earthquake affects people, animals, and nature, and the mountains, cliffs, and walls collapse.

The LORD calls for the sword against Gog’s armies, and the warriors turn against one another. Alongside this internal fighting, the passage describes plague, bloodshed, torrential rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur. As a result, the nations will know the LORD.
